title: Reading News
intro: A back-to-school issue: a new Children's Laureate, a £50,000 prize for books aimed at 8 to 12-year-olds, MPs asking for a library in every primary, a Horrible History of football, and Biff, Chip and Kipper quietly turning forty.

items.headline: Before Mildred there was Peace at Last, and it suits a new Reception class
items.author: Jill Murphy
items.book: A Bad Spell for the Worst Witch
items.summary: The Worst Witch is still the most-read series across our schools, but Murphy wrote for much younger readers too. Peace at Last (1980), Whatever Next! (1983) and Five Minutes' Peace (1986) are read-alouds a new Reception or Year 1 class can meet in September, and Five Minutes' Peace alone has sold over five million copies. Publishers turned The Worst Witch down at first. They told Murphy a school for witches would frighten children.

items.headline: Biff, Chip and Kipper turn forty this year
items.author: Roderick Hunt
items.summary: Oxford University Press has published the Oxford Reading Tree since 1986, which makes 2026 the fortieth year of Roderick Hunt's stories and Alex Brychta's pictures. Most of the reads logged across our schools are the early levels, where the magic key first appears. If you fancy marking it, four decades of children following that key is an easy assembly, and Oxford Owl has a free ebook library for home reading.

items.headline: The football season is back, and so is the reader who only reads football
items.author: Rob Childs
items.summary: Rob Childs was a Leicestershire teacher who coached school football, cricket and cross-country before he wrote any of this, which is why the matches read like someone who has stood on the touchline. The Big Match books are still in print with Penguin alongside the County Cup series. They are short and fast, built for the child who has decided reading is not for them, and September is when they work best.

items.headline: Michael Morpurgo's memoir is out on 17 September, about the farm behind Farm Boy
items.author: Michael Morpurgo
items.summary: Down Burrow Lane is Morpurgo's account of fifty years on a remote Devon farm, the one that gave him War Horse, Private Peaceful and Farm Boy. He and Clare moved there as a young schoolteacher and his wife, and their charity Farms for City Children has since welcomed more than 100,000 city children to the same fields. It turns fifty this year too. Hachette publishes the book in hardback at £20 on 17 September.

items.headline: Seventeen Roman Mysteries, a BBC series, and a free set of teaching notes
items.author: Caroline Lawrence
items.summary: The Enemies of Jupiter is book seven of seventeen, so a child who has just finished it has ten more to go, and the whole run was televised by the BBC in 2007 and 2008. Lawrence's own site has teaching resources for the series and details of school visits, and her latest book, Pantheon (2024), is a companion to the characters of Greek myth for the reader who wants to move from Romans to Greeks.

items.headline: Horrible Histories has done football, in time for the World Cup
items.author: Terry Deary
items.summary: Horrible Histories: Football came out from Scholastic on 7 May, illustrated by Martin Brown, and runs from the medieval game with no rules beyond not deliberately killing the other side to the Christmas Day match of 1914. For the child who has read every Awful, Terrible and Vile volume and now only wants to talk about the World Cup, this is the bridge. Paperback, ISBN 9780702344800.

events.name: Roald Dahl Day, his 110th birthday
events.blurb: Dahl was born in Llandaff on 13 September 1916, so this is the 110th. It lands on a Sunday, which makes the Friday before the obvious day to do something about it.

events.name: Julia Donaldson's birthday
events.blurb: Born 16 September 1948, and still the safest bet in any infant classroom. Three days after Roald Dahl Day, if you would rather run one story week than two separate things.

events.name: National Poetry Day
events.blurb: Thursday 1 October, and this year's theme is wonder. The National Literacy Trust has free classroom resources, and the day is partnered with Michael Rosen and Hot Poets on climate and poetry.

events.name: Michael Morpurgo's birthday
events.blurb: Born 5 October 1943, so he turns 83 a few weeks after Down Burrow Lane comes out. A neat excuse to put War Horse or Farm Boy in front of an upper key stage 2 class.

events.name: Green Libraries Week
events.blurb: Wednesday 21 to Wednesday 28 October, CILIP's climate-themed week for libraries. This year it is about climate facts and spotting misinformation, which is a ready-made non-fiction lesson if your local library is running something.

events.name: National Non-Fiction November
events.blurb: The whole of November, run by the Federation of Children's Book Groups. The child who will not touch a story but knows every fact about sharks gets a month where that counts as reading. World Nursery Rhyme Week sits inside it, 9 to 13 November, for the youngest.

general.label: Reading news
general.text: Patrice Lawrence MBE is the new Waterstones Children's Laureate, the fourteenth, announced on 7 July 2026 and in post until 2028. She follows Frank Cottrell-Boyce, and her theme is shared and sociable reading rather than reading alone.

general.label: Reading news
general.text: The Booker Prize Foundation has launched a Children's Booker Prize for fiction aimed at 8 to 12-year-olds. The winner takes £50,000, each of the eight shortlisted authors gets £2,500, and three children sit on the panel that picks the winner. Frank Cottrell-Boyce chairs the first jury. Shortlist in late November 2026, winner in February 2027.

general.label: Worth knowing
general.text: The cross-party Education Committee reported on 17 July 2026 that every state primary and secondary should have a funded library by law, that every child in England should get a library card at birth, and that the government should commit to a National Reading Guarantee from birth to 18.
general.source: National Literacy Trust, on the Education Select Committee report

general.label: Did you know?
general.text: The autumn term of the National Year of Reading has the theme The Community: schools working with parents and the local public library rather than doing reading alone. The National Literacy Trust's toolkits and webinars are free, and you can join partway through.
